text: Chemical disorder creates a materials design problem that cannot be solved by brute-force enumeration. A multicomponent material can adopt an enormous number of compositions and atomic configurations, each with different energies and local chemical environments. We develop AI and physics-based models that learn from this space and generate candidate materials, atomic configurations, and synthesis routes. We then test those predictions experimentally.

Our goal is not simply to predict the properties of materials that already exist. We want to generate materials with the chemistry, disorder, and local atomic environments needed for a target function. Hydrogen production and nuclear materials are where we are proving this approach.

directions.title: Hydrogen production
text: We design materials for electrochemical and thermochemical hydrogen production. For electrocatalysis, we developed machine-learning and first-principles disorder descriptors that identified platinum-free candidates from a chemical space of more than 20,000 high-entropy alloys. With experimental partners we showed that the arrangement of atoms on an alloy surface, at fixed composition and electronic structure, switches methanol oxidation activity on and off.

For thermochemical water splitting, we work with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory and Sandia National Laboratories on multi-cation oxides. These oxides release oxygen when heated and recover it from steam at lower temperatures than conventional oxide cycles. A provisional patent covers the resulting catalyst designs. The central problem is which phases in these oxides store the exchangeable oxygen and how much of it a practical cycle can recover.

directions.title: Materials for fission and fusion
text: Iodine-129 is long-lived and mobile, and few durable waste forms can immobilize it. We showed that iodine substitutes into an oxyfluoride pyrochlore and then evaluated more than 40,000 multi-cation pyrochlore compositions for higher loading, with many candidates above 33 wt% iodine. That work is part of an ARPA-E program on high-entropy glass-ceramics for waste immobilization and led to a provisional patent on iodine-bearing glass-based waste forms.

Standard density functional theory misplaces the ground states of many iodides. The group therefore builds experiment-grounded thermodynamic corrections and learns them with graph neural networks, so that calibrated energetics extend to compounds no one has measured.

For fusion, projects funded by the Seaver Institute and ARPA-E address mirrors for harsh plasma-facing environments and the cesium problem in negative hydrogen ion sources. An Air Force program studies refractory multi-principal-element alloys for extreme temperatures.

directions.title: Learning and generating configurational disorder
text: A disordered material cannot be represented by a single atomic structure. Its properties depend on an ensemble of configurations whose populations change with composition and temperature. Explicitly calculating every relevant configuration is impossible for all but the simplest systems. We develop AI models that learn these configurational spaces and generate the structures needed to predict finite-temperature materials behavior.

The aim is to move beyond brute-force screening. Rather than enumerate every possible material or atomic arrangement, we want models that learn the underlying chemical and configurational space well enough to generate candidates directly.

A first-principles database of high-entropy oxides, paired with their ordered precursors and queried through a large-language-model interface, maps which compositions form. Large-language-model extraction of synthesis routes from the literature, with explicit tracking of which conditions a paper reports, connects those compositions to how they are made. Machine-learned interatomic potentials for oxides, iodides, and alloys supply the configurational sampling. In our benchmarks, structural agreement with DFT does not necessarily imply agreement in the calculated density of states. Ongoing work examines transferability of these potentials to molecular dynamics and develops descriptors for lattice thermal conductivity and for thermal motion in diffraction.
